summary.text: Writing \(c_k=4\cos^2(\pi k/13)=2+2\cos(2\pi k/13)\), product-to-sum identities together with cosine periodicity and reflection reduce all elementary symmetric sums in the \(c_k\) to affine expressions in \(\sum_{k=1}^6\cos(2\pi k/13)\); a telescoping sine identity gives this sum as \(-\tfrac12\). Consequently those symmetric sums are \(11,45,84,70,21,1\), and expanding \(\prod_{k=1}^6(1-c_kx)\) gives the claimed polynomial.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P(x)=1-11x+45x^2-84x^3+70x^4-21x^5+x^6.
\]
We prove that
\[
P(x)=\prod_{k=1}^{6}\left(1-4\cos^2\!\left(\frac{k\pi}{13}\right)x\right).
\]

The key is first to find the polynomial whose roots are the six numbers
\(4\cos^2(k\pi/13)\).

Define polynomials \(S_n(Y)\) by
\[
S_0(Y)=2,\qquad S_1(Y)=Y,
\]
and, for \(n\ge 2\),
\[
S_n(Y)=Y S_{n-1}(Y)-S_{n-2}(Y).
\]
If \(z\ne 0\) and \(Y=z+z^{-1}\), then
\[
S_n(Y)=z^n+z^{-n}
\]
for every \(n\ge 0\). Indeed, this is clear for \(n=0,1\), and
\[
(z+z^{-1})(z^{n-1}+z^{-(n-1)})-(z^{n-2}+z^{-(n-2)})
=z^n+z^{-n},
\]
which proves the assertion inductively.

The recurrence gives, successively,
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_1(Y)&=Y,\\
S_2(Y)&=Y^2-2,\\
S_3(Y)&=Y^3-3Y,\\
S_4(Y)&=Y^4-4Y^2+2,\\
S_5(Y)&=Y^5-5Y^3+5Y,\\
S_6(Y)&=Y^6-6Y^4+9Y^2-2.
\end{aligned}
\]

Now fix an integer \(k\) with \(1\le k\le 6\), and put
\[
z=\exp\left(\frac{2\pi i k}{13}\right).
\]
Then \(z^{13}=1\), while \(z\ne 1\), because \(k\) is not divisible by \(13\). Hence the geometric-series identity gives
\[
1+z+z^2+\cdots+z^{12}=\frac{z^{13}-1}{z-1}=0.
\]
Pairing the term \(z^j\) with \(z^{13-j}=z^{-j}\), for \(j=1,\ldots,6\), yields
\[
1+\sum_{j=1}^{6}(z^j+z^{-j})=0.
\]
Set
\[
y=z+z^{-1}=2\cos\left(\frac{2\pi k}{13}\right).
\]
By the defining property of the polynomials \(S_j\), the preceding relation is
\[
1+S_1(y)+S_2(y)+S_3(y)+S_4(y)+S_5(y)+S_6(y)=0.
\]
Substituting the explicit formulas for the \(S_j\)'s and collecting like powers gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
0={}&1+y+(y^2-2)+(y^3-3y)+(y^4-4y^2+2)\\
&+(y^5-5y^3+5y)+(y^6-6y^4+9y^2-2)\\
={}&y^6+y^5-5y^4-4y^3+6y^2+3y-1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus every number
\[
y_k=2\cos\left(\frac{2\pi k}{13}\right),\qquad 1\le k\le 6,
\]
is a root of
\[
F(Y)=Y^6+Y^5-5Y^4-4Y^3+6Y^2+3Y-1.
\]

We now translate these roots. Define
\[
c_k=4\cos^2\left(\frac{k\pi}{13}\right).
\]
The double-angle identity \(2\cos^2\theta=1+\cos(2\theta)\) gives
\[
c_k=2+2\cos\left(\frac{2\pi k}{13}\right)=2+y_k.
\]
Consequently, each \(c_k\) is a root of the translated polynomial
\[
G(T)=F(T-2).
\]
A direct binomial expansion gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
G(T)
&=(T-2)^6+(T-2)^5-5(T-2)^4-4(T-2)^3\\
&\qquad +6(T-2)^2+3(T-2)-1\\
&=T^6-11T^5+45T^4-84T^3+70T^2-21T+1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
G(c_k)=0\qquad (k=1,\ldots,6).
\]

These six roots are distinct. Indeed, the angles
\[
\frac{2\pi}{13},\frac{4\pi}{13},\ldots,\frac{12\pi}{13}
\]
are strictly increasing and all lie in \((0,\pi)\). Since cosine is strictly decreasing on \([0,\pi]\), the numbers
\(y_k=2\cos(2\pi k/13)\), and hence also the numbers \(c_k=2+y_k\), are pairwise distinct.

Both \(G(T)\) and
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{6}(T-c_k)
\]
are monic polynomials of degree six, and the latter's six distinct roots are all roots of \(G\). Hence
\[
G(T)=\prod_{k=1}^{6}(T-c_k).
\]
For completeness, this follows because the difference of these two monic degree-six polynomials has degree at most five but vanishes at the six distinct values \(c_1,\ldots,c_6\); a nonzero polynomial of degree at most five cannot have six distinct roots.

Thus we have established
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{6}(T-c_k)
=T^6-11T^5+45T^4-84T^3+70T^2-21T+1.
\]
Equivalently, comparison with the standard expansion in elementary symmetric sums shows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_k c_k&=11,\\
\sum_{i<j}c_ic_j&=45,\\
\sum_{i<j<\ell}c_ic_jc_\ell&=84,\\
\sum_{i<j<\ell<m}c_ic_jc_\ell c_m&=70,\\
\sum_{i_1<\cdots<i_5}c_{i_1}\cdots c_{i_5}&=21,\\
c_1c_2c_3c_4c_5c_6&=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Expanding \(\prod_{k=1}^6(1-c_kx)\) by the same elementary symmetric sums therefore gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\prod_{k=1}^6(1-c_kx)
&=1-\left(\sum_kc_k\right)x
 +\left(\sum_{i<j}c_ic_j\right)x^2
 -\left(\sum_{i<j<\ell}c_ic_jc_\ell\right)x^3\\
&\quad+\left(\sum_{i<j<\ell<m}c_ic_jc_\ell c_m\right)x^4
 -\left(\sum_{i_1<\cdots<i_5}c_{i_1}\cdots c_{i_5}\right)x^5
 +(c_1\cdots c_6)x^6\\
&=1-11x+45x^2-84x^3+70x^4-21x^5+x^6.
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally substituting \(c_k=4\cos^2(k\pi/13)\) proves
\[
\boxed{
1-11x+45x^2-84x^3+70x^4-21x^5+x^6
=\prod_{k=1}^{6}\left(1-4\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi k}{13}\right)x\right).
}
\]
